items.prompt_md: What is the time complexity of `x in my_list` for a Python list of n items?
options: O(1), because Python hashes list items
O(n), because it scans elements one by one until it finds a match
O(log n), because lists are kept sorted
O(n^2), because each element is compared to every other
items.answer: O(n), because it scans elements one by one until it finds a match
items.explanation_md: A list has no hash index, so membership is a linear scan. Only set and dict give O(1) average lookups.

items.prompt_md: Why is `list.pop(0)` O(n) but `list.pop()` O(1)?
options: Removing the first item forces every remaining item to shift left by one slot
pop(0) must also sort the list
pop() skips the bounds check
pop(0) allocates a brand new list every time
items.answer: Removing the first item forces every remaining item to shift left by one slot
items.explanation_md: A contiguous array removes from the end for free, but removing at the front shifts all later items. A deque's popleft avoids the shift.

items.prompt_md: What is the cost of the slice `a[i:j]` in Python?
options: O(1), because it returns a view
O(n), always the full length of a
O(log n), because it uses binary search for the bounds
O(j - i), because it builds a new list copying those elements
items.answer: O(j - i), because it builds a new list copying those elements
items.explanation_md: Python slices copy. That means slicing inside a loop or in recursion can quietly turn linear work into quadratic.

items.prompt_md: Why is building a string with `s += ch` in a loop considered potentially O(n^2) in the worst case?
options: Each += triggers a sort of the characters
Python strings store characters in a linked list
Strings are immutable, so each concatenation may copy the whole string built so far
The loop variable ch is copied n times
items.answer: Strings are immutable, so each concatenation may copy the whole string built so far
items.explanation_md: Copying 1 + 2 + ... + n characters totals about n^2 / 2. Collecting pieces in a list and calling `''.join` once is O(n).

items.prompt_md: What is the preferred way to build a long string from n small pieces?
options: Use += on the string in a loop
Append the pieces to a list and call `''.join(parts)` once at the end
Insert each piece at index 0 of a list
Sort the pieces and add them with +
items.answer: Append the pieces to a list and call `''.join(parts)` once at the end
items.explanation_md: `join` computes the final length and copies each piece once: O(total length). Repeated concatenation can recopy the growing result.

items.prompt_md: Which data structure gives O(1) removal from the front, suitable for a queue?
options: `collections.deque` using `popleft()`
A Python list using `pop(0)`
A sorted list using `remove`
A string using slicing
items.answer: `collections.deque` using `popleft()`
items.explanation_md: A deque is a doubly-ended structure, so both ends are O(1). `list.pop(0)` shifts all items and is O(n).

items.prompt_md: Membership in a Python `set` is O(1) on average. What does 'on average' mean here?
options: It is O(1) only when the set has under 1000 items
It is O(log n) normally and O(1) sometimes
It is O(1) for strings but O(n) for numbers
Hash collisions can degrade a single lookup, but with a good hash the expected cost is constant
items.answer: Hash collisions can degrade a single lookup, but with a good hash the expected cost is constant
items.explanation_md: Expected constant time relies on hashing spreading items out; adversarial collisions are the rare worst case. Size alone does not break it.

items.prompt_md: A function runs `for x in a: if x in b: ...` where `a` has n items and `b` is a list of m items. What does this cost?
options: O(n), because there is one loop
O(n + m), because both lists are visited once
O(n * m), because the `in` on a list scans up to m items for each of the n iterations
O(m), because only the list is searched
items.answer: O(n * m), because the `in` on a list scans up to m items for each of the n iterations
items.explanation_md: A line inside a loop multiplies by the loop count. Converting `b` to a set first makes it O(n + m).

items.prompt_md: `sorted(words)` is called once on a list of n short words. What is its time cost?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
items.answer: O(n log n)
items.explanation_md: Comparison sorting costs n log n. Calling `sorted` is a single line but not a linear one; sorting inside a loop multiplies the cost.

items.prompt_md: Jewels and Stones with `jewels` as a string and a loop over `stones` using `if ch in jewels`. What is the time?
options: O(j * s), since each membership test may scan all j jewels
O(s), because there is a single loop
O(j + s), because each string is visited once
O(s log j), because the jewels are searched
items.answer: O(j * s), since each membership test may scan all j jewels
items.explanation_md: `in` on a string scans it, so each of s stones can cost up to j comparisons.

items.prompt_md: After converting `jewels` to a set once, what are the time and extra space for the whole counting solution?
options: O(j * s) time and O(1) space
O(s) time and O(s) space
O(j + s) time and O(j + s) space
O(j + s) time and O(j) extra space
items.answer: O(j + s) time and O(j) extra space
items.explanation_md: Building the set is O(j), each of s lookups is O(1) average, and the set holds at most j characters.

items.prompt_md: A recursive helper does `helper(arr[1:])` until the list is empty, with O(1) other work per call. What is the total time for n items?
options: O(n), because there are n calls
O(n log n), because the recursion shrinks
O(n^2), because the slices copy n-1, n-2, ... elements
O(2^n), because every call slices
items.answer: O(n^2), because the slices copy n-1, n-2, ... elements
items.explanation_md: Each slice is O(remaining length), and the lengths sum to about n^2 / 2. Passing an index avoids the copying.

items.prompt_md: Given two lists of numbers, return the values that appear in both, ignoring duplicates, for lists of 10^5 items.
options: For each item, scan the other list with `in`
Put one list in a set and check each item of the other against it
Slide a window across both lists
Recurse and slice both lists
items.answer: Put one list in a set and check each item of the other against it
items.explanation_md: Membership is the repeated question, so hash it: O(a + b). Nested scans are O(a * b), which is about 10^10 here.

items.prompt_md: You want to count how many characters of a long text are also present in a small allowed-character string.
options: Hash the allowed characters into a set and test each text character
Sort the text first and then binary search each allowed character
Reverse the text and compare from the end
Use a monotonic stack
items.answer: Hash the allowed characters into a set and test each text character
items.explanation_md: A set turns each membership question into O(1). Sorting the text adds n log n for no benefit.

items.prompt_md: A queue receives up to 10^6 items and you repeatedly remove from the front while adding at the back.
options: Use a list with `pop(0)`
Use a sorted list and `remove`
Rebuild the list by slicing after each removal
Use a deque so both ends are O(1)
items.answer: Use a deque so both ends are O(1)
items.explanation_md: The deque is the right container for FIFO access: O(1) at each end. List front removal costs O(n) each time, O(n^2) overall.

items.prompt_md: Reverse the order of words in a sentence, collapsing extra spaces, and the sentence can hold 10^5 characters.
options: Repeatedly build the answer with `result = word + ' ' + result`
Recurse on slices of the sentence
Split into words, reverse the list, and join once
Sort the words alphabetically
items.answer: Split into words, reverse the list, and join once
items.explanation_md: Split-reverse-join is O(n). Prepending to a growing string in a loop re-copies the result each time and drifts toward O(n^2).

items.prompt_md: Given a sorted list of 10^5 numbers and many queries asking if a value exists, with no extra memory allowed.
options: Convert to a set for every query
Binary search each query on the sorted list
Scan linearly for each query
Recurse with slices of the list
items.answer: Binary search each query on the sorted list
items.explanation_md: Sorted and memory-constrained points to O(log n) per query. A new set per query would be O(n) each.

items.prompt_md: Find whether any two numbers in an unsorted list add to a target, list size 10^5, memory is plentiful.
options: One pass with a hash set of numbers seen so far
Nested loops with `in` on the list for the complement
Sort then recurse with slices
Binary search the target
items.answer: One pass with a hash set of numbers seen so far
items.explanation_md: Complement lookup in a set is O(1) per element, giving O(n). Using `target - x in nums` on a list hides an O(n) scan per element.

items.prompt_md: Find the longest substring of a text with no repeated characters, testing each new character for membership in the current stretch.
options: Check each substring from scratch with nested loops
Sort the characters then scan
Recurse and slice at each repeated character
Sliding window with a set or map of the characters in the window
items.answer: Sliding window with a set or map of the characters in the window
items.explanation_md: A window plus O(1) membership gives O(n). Re-checking every substring is O(n^2) or worse, and the real structure is the shrinking and growing window.

items.prompt_md: A function needs to glue together n small strings into one big result, appending pieces one after another.
options: Use += in a loop and trust the interpreter
Insert each piece at the front of a list
Collect the pieces in a list and join once
Binary search for the insertion point of each piece
items.answer: Collect the pieces in a list and join once
items.explanation_md: A final `join` copies every character once. Repeated += can recopy the growing result. This is a string-building cost question, not a searching one.

items.prompt_md: Choose the data structure for checking 'seen before' on up to 10^6 integer IDs in a loop.
options: A list
A hash set
A sorted list with `remove`
A string of concatenated IDs
items.answer: A hash set
items.explanation_md: A set gives O(1) average membership and insertion. A list or string would need an O(n) scan for every check.

items.prompt_md: For a list of 10^5 words, group together words that are letter-rearrangements of each other.
options: Hash each word's sorted-letters (or count) signature into a dictionary of lists
Compare every pair of words with `in` checks
Binary search the word list
Slide a window over the words
items.answer: Hash each word's sorted-letters (or count) signature into a dictionary of lists
items.explanation_md: Grouping by key is hash-map work: O(n * k log k) with a sorted-letters key. Pairwise comparison is O(n^2 * k).
